section_summary: This final section combines statistical tables on exports and munitions licenses with State Department memoranda and reports concerning aircraft, petroleum, bombs, machine guns, scrap metal, and other supplies reaching Japan. It also contains congressional resolutions and speeches advocating economic sanctions, embargoes, and international action against Japanese aggression in China. The closing documents consist largely of citizens’ appeals to President Roosevelt, newspaper enclosures describing wartime suffering, and departmental replies explaining the Neutrality Act and the absence of legal authority to prohibit many exports.

subfiles.title: Statistical tables on exports and munitions-export licenses to the Far East
subfiles.about: Tables compare American commodity exports to Kwantung, China, and Hong Kong and the value of munitions licenses issued for shipments to China, Hong Kong, and Japan.
subfiles.summary: The first table continues from an earlier page and gives monthly and annual quantities of vehicles, petroleum, cotton, copper, lumber, aircraft, tobacco, flour, and related commodities. A second table lists the value of Munitions Control Office licenses, including aircraft categories, from late 1935 through October 1937.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Glenn L. Martin Company refusal of Japanese aircraft order
subfiles.from: Department of State, Arms and Munitions Control (Charles W. Yost)
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a memorandum concerning the Glenn L. Martin Company’s refusal to sell sixty military airplanes to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Mr. Hartson reports Glenn L. Martin refused a Japanese order for sixty aircraft, citing existing contracts but really unwilling to sell to Japan.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the Glenn L. Martin Company’s refusal to sell aircraft to Japan
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, with departmental routing
subfiles.about: Yost reports a telephone conversation with Mr. Hartson about a rejected Japanese order for sixty military airplanes.
subfiles.summary: Hartson says Glenn L. Martin told Japan existing contracts prevented early delivery, privately explaining it was unwilling to sell to Japan then.

subfiles.title: Letter urging an embargo on iron ore and other goods destined for Japan
subfiles.about: An iron-ore owner asks the President to stop shipments to Japan because he fears his high-sulfur ore may be used in bombs.
subfiles.summary: Christman says royalties from a new market for his low-grade ore help him, but its brittle iron could serve for mines or bombs; unable to refuse sales, he asks for an embargo on iron and other goods to Japan. A Far Eastern Affairs note follows.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: proposed sale of Foreign Refinoil patents to the United States
subfiles.from: Department of State, Legal Adviser’s Office (Flournoy)
subfiles.about: The sheet records Foreign Refinoil Company’s proposal that the United States buy patents for machinery also sought by Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Mrs. M. P. Cabell says Foreign Refinoil machines were patented in the U.S. in 1930; Japan reportedly offered $2,000,000, which the company would refuse if the U.S. bought the domestic patents.

subfiles.title: House Joint Resolution 517 authorizing economic sanctions against Japan
subfiles.from: Representative David J. Lewis of Maryland
subfiles.about: The resolution would authorize the President, in cooperation with other nations, to impose embargoes and other economic sanctions on Japan.
subfiles.summary: The preamble declares that American supplies were assisting Japan’s aggression against China in violation of the Nine Power Treaty and Kellogg-Briand Pact. It argues that the Neutrality Act was inapplicable and authorizes embargoes on munitions and other useful materials, restrictions on credits, and broader economic sanctions intended to restore peace.

subfiles.title: “Let’s Avert War—Economic Pressure as a Peace Measure”
subfiles.from: Representative Byron N. Scott of California
subfiles.about: Scott supports legislation authorizing suspension of economic relations with Japan and material assistance to China.
subfiles.summary: Congressional Record speech "Let's Avert War": Scott cites League and American findings that Japan violated agreements, argues trade arms Japan, presents export statistics, says a coordinated embargo would restrict its war industry, and urges House Joint Resolution 537.

subfiles.title: “Authorizing the President, in Cooperation with Other Nations, to Apply Economic Sanctions to Japan”
subfiles.doc_type: Congressional Record speech with quoted letter
subfiles.from: Representative David J. Lewis of Maryland
subfiles.about: Lewis argues for international legal institutions and economic sanctions against Japan while opposing the Ludlow war-referendum proposal.
subfiles.summary: Lewis, shaped by Joseph Harrison's pacifism and the Lusitania, argues peace needs enforceable law, criticizes isolationism and the Ludlow resolution, and endorses Roosevelt, Hull and Stimson on economic action, quoting Stimson at length on Japan's dependence on American and British materials.

subfiles.title: Corrected telegram reporting a Royal Dutch Shell gasoline contract with Japan
subfiles.about: A confidential source reports that Royal Dutch Shell contracted to supply Japan with sixty million liters of gasoline.
subfiles.summary: Corrected telegram: Royal Dutch Shell allegedly contracted to deliver gasoline to Japan by spring 1938 at eighty Dutch cents per liter, ninety for earlier delivery; the Dutch prime minister reportedly knew, and the source demanded confidentiality.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of The Hague telegram on the Shell gasoline contract
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: The memorandum paraphrases the confidential report of Japan’s contract with Royal Dutch Shell.
subfiles.summary: Paraphrase of The Hague telegram on the Shell contract: spring 1938 delivery, eighty or ninety Dutch cents per liter, the prime minister apparently aware, strictest confidentiality.

subfiles.title: Telegram 119 from The Hague on the Royal Dutch Shell gasoline contract
subfiles.about: The Legation transmits a trusted informant’s report of a sixty-million-liter gasoline sale to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Hague telegram 119: Royal Dutch Shell reportedly agreed to deliver fuel by spring 1938 with a premium for earlier delivery; the prime minister knew; source demands secrecy.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: transit of war materials through Hong Kong
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a report on the transshipment and transit of military materials at Hong Kong.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: report on war materials in transit through Hong Kong, some for China and some presumed for Japan, file 893.113/1667.

subfiles.title: Military attaché report on Italian aircraft, bombs, and personnel for Japan
subfiles.about: The report collects information on Italian aircraft, aviation personnel, bombs, and procurement arrangements associated with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Military attache: reports of an Italian ship with aircraft and personnel, later airplane bombs; Colonel Watanabe's Japanese mission visited Italian factories, and Baron Okura reportedly contracted for Italian planes, including Ba.20 bombers; quantities unknown.

subfiles.title: Report of airplane bombs aboard the S.S. Ischia for Japan
subfiles.from: Horace Remillard, American Consul, Port Said
subfiles.about: A port-control source reports that the Italian steamer Ischia carried heavy airplane bombs intended for Yokohama.
subfiles.summary: The S.S. Ischia passed Suez December 5 declaring Massawa, but a port-control officer reported it carried 1,200 deadweight tons of heavy airplane bombs for Yokohama.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: machine guns for Seversky aircraft sold to Japan
subfiles.from: Department of State, Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: The sheet references a conversation about Colt machine guns for twenty Seversky airplanes being sold to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Seversky wished to buy Colt machine guns for twenty aircraft sold to Japan; memorandum of a talk with Colt vice president H. D. Fairweather.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Italian aircraft and aviators ordered to Japan
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a telegram reporting Italian aircraft and aviators ordered to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The initial figures were eighty aircraft and fifty Italian aviators. A British colleague’s information reduced the aircraft figure to fifty.

subfiles.title: Telegram from Chiasso on Italian aircraft and airmen sent to Japan
subfiles.about: Sholes reports that Italian aircraft and airmen, some recently returned from Spain, had been ordered to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Chiasso telegram: initial report of eighty aircraft and fifty Italian airmen sent to Japan; Sholes adds a British colleague puts aircraft at fifty.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Malayan exports of war material to Japan
subfiles.about: The sheet identifies a Singapore despatch about Malayan exports of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: a London newspaper report quoted by the Straits Times on December 15 condemning Malaya's war-material exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: British war-material exports to Japan and China
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a despatch on British exports of war materials to Japan and China.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: British despatch 3890 on war-material exports to both China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Letter protesting American war-material shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: A Belmont peace advocate urges the President to stop American bombs, ammunition, and oil from reaching Japan.
subfiles.summary: A Belmont Woman's Club member protests supplying material that kills Chinese civilians while asking donations for the injured, and appeals for courageous action.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Mrs. Robert B. Eastman
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains why it had not invoked the Neutrality Act to prohibit arms exports to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost tells Mrs. Eastman a presidential finding of war under the May 1, 1937 resolution would bar arms to both countries; without it there is no authority to restrict Japan alone, and Roosevelt judged invoking it inadvisable.

subfiles.title: Letter protesting crude-oil and supply shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Mathewson asks why the United States permits crude oil and other supplies to be sent to Japan for use against Chinese civilians.
subfiles.summary: Writer frames crude-oil and supply shipments to Japan as a moral question and refers the President to enclosed newspaper material on the war's consequences.

subfiles.title: “Bombing of Hankow Told in Letter”
subfiles.about: The clipping reports S. C. Huang’s account of air raids, refugees, and civilian deaths in Hankow and Soochow.
subfiles.summary: Clipping: Huang writes to John Price of Christmas bombing and massacre, 250 noncombatants killed and 500 wounded in one Hankow raid, about 700 bombs on Soochow in thirty hours, and refugees crowding Hankow.

subfiles.title: “Far East Resident Urges Boycott”
subfiles.about: The clipping reports Mrs. Fitch’s appeal for relief work, a boycott of Japanese goods, and an embargo on strategic exports.
subfiles.summary: Mrs. Fitch tells a Kiwanis luncheon to roll bandages, boycott Japanese goods and stop crude oil, scrap and cotton exports, describing hospital bombings and the looting of her Nanking home, and warning of Japan's wider conquest.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to J. A. Mathewson
subfiles.from: Department of State, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains the statutory limits on restricting crude oil, arms, and other exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: State tells J. A. Mathewson a war finding would halt arms to China and Japan, no authority exists to restrict goods beyond arms except tin-plate scrap and helium, and the President judged invoking the resolution inadvisable.

subfiles.title: Letter from Rudolph Dufka about scrap steel sent to Japan
subfiles.about: A twelve-year-old asks why scrap steel intended for Japan cannot be retained for American armaments.
subfiles.summary: Rudolph Dufka sends a Herald and Examiner picture of scrap steel bound for Japan, admits the caption may be propaganda, and says the steel should stay in the U.S.

subfiles.title: Photograph caption: freight cars of scrap steel for Japan
subfiles.about: A caption states that freight cars loaded with scrap steel intended for Japan fell through a pier at San Pedro.
subfiles.summary: Photo caption: four freight cars of scrap steel for Japan made a large splash after a pier collapsed.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Rudolph Dufka
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains that the President lacked statutory authority to prohibit exports of iron and steel scrap to Japan.
subfiles.summary: State tells Dufka a presidential war finding would require an arms embargo on both belligerents; scrap isn't arms, and Roosevelt judged invoking the resolution not in U.S. interests.
